opus-5.5.text:
Well, the starting point is that the classical definition of rationality — perfect rationality, where the agent always chooses the action that maximizes expected utility given what it knows — is simply not achievable. The computations involved are intractable for any interesting environment. So if you define the goal of AI as building perfectly rational agents, you've defined a goal that nobody can ever reach, and it doesn't give you much guidance about what to do instead.

Bounded optimality shifts the question. Instead of asking "what's the best action?", you ask "what's the best *program* for this particular machine, running in this particular class of environments?" The machine has finite speed and finite memory, and the environment doesn't wait for you while you think. So the designer's job is to find the agent program that, when actually executed on that hardware, produces the best expected performance over the distribution of environments it will face. That's a well-defined optimization problem, and crucially, a solution always exists — there's always some best program, even if we don't know how to find it.

What changes for the designer is that you stop thinking of deliberation as free. Time spent computing is time not acting, and the value of a computation has to be weighed against its cost. That leads naturally to things like metareasoning — rational control of your own computations, deciding which bit of thinking is actually worth doing — and to anytime algorithms, compilation of knowledge into fast reflexes, and so on. A bounded-optimal agent might be quite "irrational" in the classical sense in particular instances, because it's using shortcuts, but those shortcuts are the right ones given its constraints.

It also changes how you evaluate things. You're not grading individual decisions; you're grading the whole agent design over its lifetime of experience. That's much closer to how we should think about evolution, or learning, or engineering practice generally.

And I'd add one thing that's become more important to me over time: bounded optimality is still optimality *with respect to some objective*. It tells you how to pursue a goal well under computational limits, but it says nothing about whether the goal is the right one. So in the broader picture, I think the designer has to optimize not for a fixed objective that we write down, but for being genuinely beneficial to humans — which means the machine has to be uncertain about what we want and has to learn it. Bounded optimality is about the "how"; the harder and more important question is the "what."

r001.rationale: It defines bounded optimality as choosing the program that performs best when executed on a particular finite machine across its environments.

r002.rationale: It frames the designer’s task as finding and evaluating the whole agent program, rather than optimizing each individual action.

r003.rationale: It says shortcuts can be right given constraints, but does not state that correcting a locally suboptimal action would worsen the program’s overall performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that it moves the target from "the optimal action" to "the optimal program," and that turns out to be a much more honest thing to aim at.

The classical picture, which goes back to Von Neumann and Morgenstern and then into AI through the idea of the rational agent, says you should pick the action that maximizes expected utility. That's a lovely definition, and it's also impossible to implement. Real agents have finite memory, finite time, finite compute. A chess-playing program that tried to compute the perfectly rational move would never move. So if you tell a designer "build a perfectly rational agent," you've given them a specification that no physical object can satisfy, and then they're left quietly making compromises without any theory about which compromises are good.

Bounded optimality, which Eric Horvitz and I and others worked on in the late eighties and nineties, says: fix the machine. Fix the architecture, the clock speed, the memory. Now ask, of all the programs that could run on that machine, which one produces the best expected behavior in the environments it's going to face? That is a well-defined optimization problem. The answer exists. It's an agent program, not an action. And crucially the program will sometimes do things that look locally irrational, like truncate a search, or use a crude heuristic, because the cost of thinking more would exceed the value of the improved decision. Those aren't failures. They're part of what it means to be optimal under the constraint.

So what changes for the designer? A few things.

First, you stop treating computation as free. Deliberation itself becomes an action with a cost and an expected benefit, and the agent should be reasoning, at least implicitly, about which computations are worth doing. That's the metareasoning idea, and it shows up all over the place now: anytime algorithms, Monte Carlo tree search deciding where to expand, even the early-exit tricks in large models.

Second, you optimize over families of programs rather than trying to directly hand-craft decision rules. You're choosing a design, and the design's quality is measured by performance in the world, not by how closely it resembles the ideal Bayesian agent. That's actually quite close to what machine learning does in practice, which is part of why I think the framework has aged well.

Third, and this is the part I think people underrate, it forces you to be explicit about the environment class. A boundedly optimal program is optimal relative to the distribution of situations it will encounter. If you get that wrong, the program is optimized for the wrong world. Which connects, I'd say, to my later preoccupations with uncertainty about objectives. If the designer admits they don't know the environment perfectly, they should also be willing to admit they don't know the objective perfectly, and build agents that treat both as things to be learned rather than fixed in advance.

So the one-sentence version: bounded optimality says don't optimize the decision, optimize the decision-maker, given what it's made of and where it's going to live. Once you take that seriously, a lot of what looks like engineering hackery turns out to be the theory, not a deviation from it.

r001.rationale: It defines bounded optimality as choosing the best-performing program among those that can run on a fixed machine.

r002.rationale: It contrasts optimizing the program or decision-maker with optimizing an individual action.

r003.rationale: It explains that extra thinking can cost more than the improved decision is worth, so replacing the program’s locally suboptimal choice with a seemingly better one can reduce overall performance.

astra-6.text:
Well, it shifts the object of optimization from an individual action to the program that produces actions. In the usual idealization, we ask what a perfectly rational agent would do, as though computation were instantaneous and free. But a real agent has a particular machine, a limited amount of memory, and a limited amount of time. Thinking has a cost: while you’re computing the perfect answer, the opportunity to act may disappear.

Bounded optimality asks: of all the programs that could run on this machine, which one produces the best expected performance in the environments we care about? That program may use approximations, shortcuts, or habits. Those aren’t necessarily defects; they may be precisely what makes it the best program given its constraints.

So the designer’s task is to optimize the agent’s overall behavior, including how it spends its computational resources. You’re not trying to make every decision theoretically perfect. You’re trying to build the best decision-making system that the available machinery can support.

r001.rationale: It asks which executable program produces the best expected performance on a particular machine with limited resources.

r002.rationale: It says optimization shifts from individual actions to the program that produces them.

r003.rationale: It says shortcuts may be best under constraints, but does not explain that correcting a locally suboptimal action would worsen the program’s overall performance.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, it shifts the object of optimization from an individual action to the program that produces actions. In the usual account of rationality, you ask, “What’s the best action, given everything the agent has observed?” But finding that action may require more computation than you could possibly carry out before you have to act.

Bounded optimality asks instead: “What’s the best program we can run on the machine we actually have?” You evaluate that program by how well it does in the environments it will encounter, including the consequences of the time it spends thinking. A program that eventually finds a wonderful answer may be much worse than one that finds a reasonably good answer while there’s still time to use it.

So the designer should optimize the agent’s overall behavior under its computational constraints. That includes how it allocates computation, when it stops deliberating, and what it learns to do quickly. The limitations aren’t an unfortunate qualification added to the theory afterward; they’re part of the design problem itself.

r001.rationale: It identifies the best program runnable on the machine available and evaluates it by performance under its computational constraints.

r002.rationale: It contrasts optimizing an individual action with optimizing the program that produces actions, and says the designer should optimize the agent’s overall behavior.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that correcting a locally suboptimal action could worsen the program’s overall performance.
